Kharkiv Newest Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kharkiv Oblast, Ukraine

Not demolished. Kharkiv fell beyond the Pale of Settlement, so Jews were officially barred from living there except as cantonists discharged from military service or as merchants, who formed two separate congregations. In 1882, Kharkiv students founded Bilu, one of the earliest Zionist groups to actually settle in Palestine, and the city remained a major Zionist center until the 1920s. Unusually for Ukraine, Kharkiv did not experience a pogrom during the 1917 revolutions or the Civil War that followed, and the city served as the capital of Soviet Ukraine from 1919 to 1934. By 1939, Kharkiv's Jewish population had reached 130,250. Most were able to evacuate before the German capture in October 1941; around 10,000 remaining Jews were forced into a ghetto that December, and the majority were killed at Drobytskyi Yar in January 1942, while about 400 sick or elderly Jews were locked in a synagogue on Meshchanskaia Street, where they died of cold and hunger. This Jewish section, with its earliest tombstone dated 1926, remains in use today, divided into men's and women's subsections.
